newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian exports to China seen secure.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian exports to China seen secure.

text.p: Australia's commodity exports to China, totalling about A$4 billion a year, appear to be secure after the death of China's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, industry officials said on Thursday.
Representatives of Australia's iron ore, wool and cotton industries, representing three of Australia's leading export commodities to China, said they did not see major disruptions.
"It's one of those unanswerable questions but we do not expect that it will have an impact," said Ian Head, spokesman for Anglo-Australian mining group RTZ-CRA.
Through its Hamersley unit, RTZ-CRA is a major exporter of iron ore to China, which imported A$570 million worth of the steelmaking material from Australia in calendar 1996.
The CRA-RTZ group is partner with China's Metallurgical Import and Export Corp in the Channar iron ore mine in Western Australia, which last year exported 7.8 million tonnes of iron ore to China.
Wool, Australia's top export to China with A$756 million sold in 1996, also appears safe from fallout from Deng's death.
Brian Clancy, corporate affairs manager for statutory authority Wool International, said he did not believe Deng's death would have an impact on wool sales.
"These sort of events ... the only time there was a hiccup in the wool industry in the past was Tiananmen Square," he said, referring to Beijing's 1989 crackdown against democracy demonstrators.
Tax crackdowns also had the potential to affect trade, but Deng's death was likely to leave trade unscathed, he said.
Textiles were an integral employer in China, Australia's top customer for Australian wool, Clancy said.
Australian wool exports to China in calendar 1996 rose by 24 percent in volume terms to 218 million kg and by six percent in value terms to A$883 million.
China takes about 30 percent of Australia's wool.

Japan, now officially rated fourth on the list of customers for Australian wool, was a force behind some China-denominated purchases of Australian wool through ownership of processing plants in Taiwan and China, he said.
"This organisation sees no hiccups in the system," he said.
A cotton industry spokeswoman, who asked not to be named, the death was unlikely to cause upheaval to trade Deng had effectively handed over power seven years ago.

David Farley, managing director of Colly Cotton Ltd, Australia's leading cotton producer and the world's second-largest integrated cotton company, said that at the moment Deng's death was not seen affecting the trade.
Farley, who often travels to China on business, said the Chinese would not be able to afford to stop the trade, even if they wished to.
